BOOK_A.title: Litigation Representative Required
BOOK_A.related_provisions: 3.36(2) (noting litigation representative in default) ; 11.7 (service on litigation representative) ; 12.6 (minors involved in family litigation)
BOOK_A.commentary:
A. Transitional
The person who was formerly called a “next friend” is now called a “litigation representative”.
There are three types, described in R.2.12.
Case law on next friends or guardians ad litem under the old Rules remains highly inﬂuential
under the new.¹
B. Estates
There is a textbook.²
An estate (by its legal personal representative) can sue on a right which the deceased had,
only if the cause of action survives; in torts cases often now it does not.³
Neither a deceased person, nor the estate of a deceased person, is a legal entity. But a suit
by “the estate of John Smith” may be amended to name an executor or administrator who existed
when the suit began.⁴
A legal entity is required to represent the estate. Ordinarily, this would be
a trustee, executor, or administrator,⁵
or an administrator ad litem under the Survival of Actions
Act⁶
or the Fatal Accidents Act.⁷
In a lawsuit (as to a contract between the deceased and Mr. A), a beneﬁciary of the estate has
no standing to sue Mr. A. That is so whether or not the motive of the beneﬁciary is self-interest. A
beneﬁciary can only claim against the executor or trustee.⁸

The Fatal Accidents Act requires that a suit under it be by an executor or administrator, but not
doing so is curable, and not a ground to strike the suit.¹
If the bankrupt’s estate will not produce a surplus, the bankrupt himself has no standing to
seek his trustee’s removal.²
In litigation about how to interpret the will of one deceased, one party was the estate of another
deceased. The latter estate was denied leave to be represented by a non-lawyer, as contrary to R.
2.11 about estates. Following R.2.11 was very important, especially as there seemed to be some
question about the latter will.³
C. Persons Lacking Capacity
On litigation representatives generally, see the Civil Procedure Encyclopedia.⁴
Minors⁵
and persons of unsound mind are often not capable of instructing counsel or
commencing actions. Someone has to do this for them.⁶
Minors, for example, may sue or
counterclaim by a litigation representative.⁷
No order is required for this, but an afﬁdavit of the
litigation representative must be ﬁled.⁸
When a litigation representative sues, the only person suing is the disabled one, and the
litigation representative or guardian is not a separate person or party. The remedy is to have terms
imposed when a litigation guardian is appointed by the court.⁹
The job of the litigation representative is to pay costs¹⁰
and to give instructions to counsel in
all matters except concluding a settlement. The litigation representative is not to run the action
without counsel, and if he attempts to do so, the court will require a replacement (e. g. , the Public
Trustee. )¹¹
The litigation representative of a minor is usually a parent, but sometimes the court
might appoint a stranger as litigation representative.¹²
He or she must be an “interested person”,
but that is not deﬁned.¹³
If there was a previous litigation representative, no formal resignation is

necessary, but proper evidence is necessary, and there must be no conﬂict of interest, and often
the Public Trustee should be consulted.¹
The court has no right to order the Public Trustee, in litigation in which he is otherwise not
involved, to provide or fund a litigation representative for a minor plaintiff, e. g. when his existing
representative has a conﬂict or does not wish to continue.²
Mentally disabled persons with no trustee or guardian under the Dependent Adults Act³
may
sue or counterclaim by a litigation representative as well. The court can determine whether there
is capacity. If a mentally incompetent adult sues by himself, the court may later add his trustee
as a plaintiff, despite a limitation period, if there is no prejudice to the defendant?⁴
But something
must be done, for appointment (by the court or operation of law) of a representative for a mentally
incompetent person takes away any capacity which that person had to bring or continue court
proceedings herself, or to appear personally in court.⁵
Minors and mentally incompetent persons may defend by a litigation representative, whom
a court may appoint if necessary.⁶
If a guardianship or trusteeship order is in place, it should be
checked to conﬁrm that it gives authority to the guardian or trustee to represent the dependent
adult in legal proceedings.
D. Types of Representative
The Public Trustee can perform these roles, though he is not often eager to act as litigation
representative if there is any suitable alternative, because of the potential exposure to costs. The
Public Trustee should be notiﬁed if a lawsuit involves the estate of a minor (e. g. , personal injury
damages), and must be notiﬁed if a court application involves the property or estate of a minor,
missing person, convict or mentally incompetent person.
A litigation representative should be indifferent as to the outcome of the proceedings, free
of conﬂict of interest, and able to give an unbiassed assessment of the legal situation and the
appropriate actions to take. When it is an estate dispute, a family member who is involved in the
dispute is not suitable, even though ordinarily family members would be suitable as litigation
representatives.⁷
In litigation over who would disburse trust fund payments for minor members
of an Indian Band, the courts preferred the Public Trustee to parents, and appointed the Public
Trustee as litigation representative.⁸
The court should appoint counsel for a child only if the parents cannot properly represent the
child’s best interests.⁹
One parent warring with the other parent over custody cannot unilaterally
appoint a lawyer for the child, and if the court were later to bless that appointment it would look
biassed. If one parent thinks that the child needs independent counsel, a motion to that effect
should be made to the court.¹⁰

The Court of King's Bench has inherent power to make an interim appointment of a person’s
guardian, in an urgent situation, even if the statutory notice periods under the Dependent Adults
Act are not met.¹
Parents are automatically the guardians of the person of a minor, but not automatically
guardians of the estate of minors.²
Parents may be appointed as guardian of the estate of a minor,
but they may be required to post a bond.
The Miscellaneous Statutes Amendment Act 1996³
made a signiﬁcant change to this area
of the law. Formerly, the Public Trustee would automatically become the guardian ad litem of
the estate of a minor, missing person, or mental incompetent once notice was given. Now court
approval is required. Therefore, one should ﬁrst determine whether a suitable representative
exists.⁴
One cannot assume that the Public Trustee will perform the role of guardian ad litem.
A suit by a trustee in bankruptcy against third parties is not within Bankruptcy Rules, and
is primarily ordinary civil litigation, even if the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act affects some of
the rights of the parties. The trustee represents the bankrupt corporation, and has no separate
existence or identity.⁵
E. Authority and Procedure
If someone is under a disability, the Limitations Act suspends operation of the Act. That could
be indeﬁnite, if the disability is likely permanent. Existence of any kind of guardian for the disabled
person is no excuse, given the statute’s clear wording.⁶
Court approval is needed for settlement.⁷
A lawyer with any doubts about his or her client’s ability to give instructions should look ﬁrst
to see if there is a Guardianship Order, a Trusteeship Order, or a Certiﬁcate of Incapacity. Or if
one is needed. Partway into a suit for personal injury, a plaintiff’s parents were appointed his
guardians and trustees, only on condition that they undertake to be responsible for costs. Security
was unnecessary because they lived in Alberta. The defendants claimed that the plaintiff had had
no mental capacity to sue, but the court found no prejudice and that the defendant knew of the
disability.⁸

If a lawyer’s client loses mental capacity, the lawyer loses authority to take steps in the existing
suit.¹
Where an infant defended himself, his statement of defence was not struck out. But there
being no exceptional circumstances, the court appointed the Public Guardian to represent him in
the suit.²
The style of cause in such an action looks like this:
Plaintiff: X, a minor, by his Litigation Representative, Y.
Defendant: A, a minor, by her Litigation Representative, B.
Unless there is an express exception in the Legal Profession Act (or the court exercises
its discretion?), a representative of a party under a disability needs a lawyer to represent the
representative. The old law on that subject continues under the new Rules. It would be pointless
to appoint a litigation representative when the whole aim was to litigate without a lawyer.³
Where a lawyer was removed from a panel of people who would be hired to represent children
because of accusations of incivility, that was not a removal of the right to practice law generally,
and arguments that there was inconsistency between the “client” (the Ofﬁce of the Children’s
Advocate) and a duty of civility, did not make sense.⁴
F. Costs
One of the main functions of a litigation representative is to answer for costs. Indeed, it may be
that he or she is primarily liable to pay costs, and can merely later try to get reimbursement from
the minor.⁵
Therefore, if a lawyer is about to issue a statement of claim for a minor, it is important
to warn the litigation representative about this liability for costs. If the litigation representative is
not the infant’s parent or guardian, and would derive no beneﬁt at all from the suit, it might be
necessary that he or she get independent advice. He or she should also be warned that he or she
must run the minor’s suit for the beneﬁt of the minor, and that any out-of court settlement must
probably be approved by the court. He or she should also be warned that if he (or she) and the
infant have, or later develop, a conﬂict of interest, the litigation representative’s own interests may
have to take second place to the infant’s.
A court-appointed representative for an infant was liable for costs incurred after she tried to
resign, because she kept acting (and later discontinued her own claim).⁶
Judicially-appointed trustees are entitled to reasonable remuneration adjusted from time to
time, based on time spent, importance of the task, and similar matters.⁷

G. Representative is Not Party
A litigation representative is not a party in his or her own right, and making him or her a party
later by amendment is the addition of a new party.¹
Guardians and trustees of an infant plaintiff are
not parties in their own right, and their counsel acts only in the interests of the infant. Therefore
an amendment shortly before trial to add allegations against them of negligence leading to the
accident would be prejudicial.²

BOOK_B.title: Litigation representative required

commentary.text: Rule 2.11 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.11. 1. Lack of Capacity under R. 2.11(c) In Chutskoff Estate v. Bonora, 2013 ABQB 119, Madam Justice Ross said, at paragraph 19: 19 The Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act, whose definition of capacity is incorporated in Rule 2.11(c), provides that “an adult is presumed to have the capacity to make decisions until the contrary is determined”: s 2(a). It is in my view appropriate to take the same approach under Rule 2.11(c). The admitted fact that the Respondent suffers from a psychiatric condition does not mean that he lacks capacity as defined in Rule 2.11(c). Lack of capacity in the defined sense must be proved on a balance of probabilities. In Alberta (Public Guardian) v. C. (K.), 2015 ABQB 369, an application was brought under the Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act (Alberta) in relation to the guardianship of a 27 year old individual (DC) suffering from Down's Syndrome who lacked “the capacity to make informed decisions relating to such matters as health care; where, with whom and under what circumstances he will live; who he may associate with; participation in social activities; participation in educational, vocational and other training; employment; and the carrying on of any legal proceedings unrelated to financial matters. His judgment and insight were further impacted by a tobogganing accident in 2009 in which he sustained head injuries.” Justice Gates concluded that DC should be permitted to be represented by counsel for the limited purpose of putting forth his/her views on the application. Justice Gates said: 65 DC was represented by counsel throughout these proceedings. Counsel advised the Court that she had been retained to make submissions to the Court with regard to DC's views and wishes. She also indicated that he did not want to participate in the proceedings by way of giving evidence or through the cross examination of any witnesses. 66 DC's counsel relied on s. 28(1) of the AGTA, which directs the Court to consider “the views and wishes of the adult, if ascertainable.” 67 Rule 2.11 of the Alberta Rules of Court directs that a Represented Adult must have a litigation representative in order to bring, defend, continue or participate in an action. However, this rule is qualified by Rule 12.6(2), which provides that a child is not considered to be participating in an action for the purposes of the Rule 2.11 merely by being the subject of the dispute or being served with notice of the proceedings. 68 I accept the argument advanced by DC's counsel that Rule 12.6(2), by analogy, applies in these circumstances so as to obviate the requirement for DC to have a litigation representative appointed to permit him to participate in this action. Like a child, DC lacks the legal capacity to either represent himself or to retain counsel for that purpose. However, he clearly has an interest in these proceedings notwithstanding that he had no role in bringing, defending, or continuing them. His proposed participation in these proceedings is a very limited one—the opportunity to express his views and wishes prior to the rendering of a decision on this application. He does not wish to participate otherwise and, indeed, does not oppose his need of a guardian or, indeed, the Public Guardian's application in this instance. 69 In my view, DC should be permitted to be represented by counsel for this very limited purpose. I would note that counsel are frequently appointed in family law cases to “represent” the views and/or wishes of children relative to legal proceedings in which they are implicated. In such instances, this information can be very helpful to the Court in determining what is in the best interest of the child or children. The same principle should, by analogy, apply here, namely that the expression of DC's views and wishes will, potentially, be very helpful to the Court in determining what is in his best interest in the future. Accordingly, I find that Rule 2.11 does not preclude DC from being represented by counsel in these proceedings so as to allow his voice to be heard. 70 During the course of these proceedings, counsel for Mr. C took the position that DC lacked the capacity to retain or instruct counsel. While this legal issue was not fully argued before me, I would offer the view that I am inclined to agree with this position. However, it seems to me that counsel may reflect the views and wishes of either a child or, as in this instance, a represented adult, without having been formally retained or instructed so long as the child or represented adult has the necessary capacity to understand the nature of the proceedings, generally, and the ability or capacity to provide instruction with regard to his or her views relative to the proceeding. 2. Litigation representative for an estate In Kunkel v. Winquist, 2022 ABQB 367, 2022 CarswellAlta 1305, Justice Leonard said: [23] However, there is nothing in the language of the Rules of Court to suggest that the litigation representative of an estate must be a person who is entitled to apply for a grant of administration. There is also nothing in the case law to suggest that the possible litigation representatives for an estate should be limited to those people who are entitled to apply for a grant of administration. [24] Instead, when appointing a litigation representative, the primary goal of the Court is to ensure the interests of the estate are represented: Hughes Estate v Hughes, 2007 ABCA 277. Most importantly, a litigation representative should not be in conflict with the interests of the estate: Rufenak v Hope Mission, 2005 ABCA 129. The litigation representative should also be able to manage the litigation and be willing to pay the court costs of the litigation: see Rules of Court, r 10.47. [25] When it comes to the relationship between a litigation representative and an estate, a beneficiary of an estate can act as the litigation representative: Lux v Lux, 2021 ABCA 413 at para 5. However, this does not need to be the case: Gonnerud (Litigation Guardians of) v Gonnerud Estate, 2002 SCC 38 at para 21. Ultimately, the driving question for the Court is whether a litigation representative will represent the interests of the estate. [26] Considering these authorities, I conclude that it is not necessary for the litigation representative of an estate to have priority to apply for a grant of administration under the Estate Administration Act. …

commentary.text:
“Represented adult” is defined in the Adult Guardian and Trusteeship Act S.A. 2008, c. A-4.2, s. 1(hh). as an adult in respect of whom a guardianship order, a trusteeship order, or both orders are in effect. Capacity is defined under thatAct to mean, in respect of the making of a decision about a matter, the ability to understand the information that is relevant to the decision and to appreciate the reasonably foreseeable consequences of both a decision, and the failure to make a decision. Adult Guardian and Trusteeship Act, S.A. 2008, c. A-4.2, s. 1(d). This definition is incorporated into rule 2.11. Lack of capacity must be proved on a balance of probabilities. Chutskoff Estate v. Bonora, [2013] A.J. No. 195, 2013 ABQB 119 at para. 19 (Alta. Q.B.).
Rule 2.11 can include situations where a personal representative is already in place arising from an appointment under a will, but a grant of probate has not yet been obtained. 1368276 Alberta Ltd. v. Grotski Estate, [2015] A.J. No. 849, 2015 ABQB 490 at para. 28 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)). It does not preclude a represented adult from being represented by counsel in proceedings where
